title: Evaluation-efficient quantum architecture search with ZX-calculus-based topological reuse
authors: Chenlu Li, Hui Zeng, Dazhi Ding
abstract: Variational quantum algorithm is a leading approach for quantum chemistry and many-body physics on noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. The performance depends strongly on the structure of the parameterized quantum circuits. Quantum architecture search (QAS) can automate ansatz design. However, it requires repeated training and evaluation of many candidate circuits, leading to high evaluation cost. In this work, we propose a noise-aware quantum architecture search framework based on ZX-calculus topological reuse (ZX-QAS). The framework encodes the search space with a ternary Gray-code mapping and integrates a noise-aware quantum neural network with a ZX-calculus topological reuse mechanism. The effectiveness of the framework is validated through ground-state energy estimation tasks and one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model tasks under noisy conditions. The results show that the ZX-QAS exhibits stable convergence and remarkably reduces the cost of expensive evaluations under noisy conditions.
summary: This paper introduces ZX-QAS, a novel, evaluation-efficient framework for Quantum Architecture Search designed for noisy quantum devices. It mitigates high computational costs by integrating ZX-calculus topological reuse with a Gray-code mapping to manage the search space. The approach successfully demonstrates stable convergence and significant cost reduction for simulating quantum many-body systems.
main_problem: Quantum Architecture Search (QAS) for Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQA) suffers from prohibitively high evaluation costs due to the need for repeated training and evaluation of many candidate circuits.
main_result: The proposed ZX-QAS framework significantly reduces the cost of expensive evaluations under noisy conditions while maintaining stable convergence for tasks like ground-state energy estimation.
method: The framework combines a noise-aware quantum neural network with a ZX-calculus topological reuse mechanism and uses a ternary Gray-code mapping to implicitly encode the search space.
model_or_system: The work targets NISQ devices applied to quantum chemistry and many-body physics, exemplified by the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model. The search space is managed using ZX-calculus graphs and a Gray-code mapping.
key_observables: Ground-state energy estimation, stable convergence, and the reduction in the number of required circuit evaluations.
important_parameters: Noise parameters (e.g., $p_{BF}$ for bit-flip, $T_1, T_2$ for relaxation), the similarity threshold for topological reuse, and the number of qubits ($N$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that structural similarity, quantifiable via ZX-calculus, can serve as an effective prior to reuse computational results and reduce the evaluation budget.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the basic graphical elements and rewrite rules of ZX-calculus, and a workflow diagram shows the three steps of the ZX-QAS framework: mapping, training, and reuse.
paper_structure: The paper first identifies the high cost of QAS, then introduces the ZX-QAS framework which uses a ternary Gray-code mapping for efficient search space encoding. It details the noise-aware training using supernets and finally leverages the ZX-calculus for topological reuse during the search process.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical limitations of applying quantum algorithms to near-term hardware by providing a computationally efficient method to explore the vast space of quantum circuits.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Basic graphical elements and rewrite rules of ZX- calculus. (a) State and phase-gate representations of Z and X spiders. Green nodes denote Z-basis spiders, and red nodes denote X-basis spiders. A single-input single-output spider with phase π corresponds to the Pauli-Z or Pauli-X opera- tion. (b) Equivalent representations of the Hadamard gate and the Hadamard edge. (c) Spider-fusion rule. (d) Color- change rule. (e) Identity-removal rule. (f) Antipode rule. ZX-calculus contains other rewrite rules, which are not listed here; see Ref. [39] for details.

FIG. 2. Workﬂow of the ZX-QAS framework. In step 1, single-qubit rotation gates are mapped to the Rs space using a ternary Gray-code mapping, and entangling gates are represented by a sparse CNOT lookup table. In step 2, a sampled ansatz is decoded and combined with the noise model, and multiple supernet experts are trained. The shared parameters are updated through an ǫ-greedy strategy. In step 3, the search inherits the noise-aware supernet parameters. During evolutionary search, each candidate ansatz is converted into a ZX graph for topological feature extraction. FIG. 3. Energy-error convergence curves. Panels (a), (b), and (c) show the results for H2, LiH, and H4, respectively. The horizontal axis denotes the evaluation step, and the vertical axis denotes the best-so-far energy error. The orange and purple curves show the results of the proposed ZX-QAS under noisy and noiseless conditions, respectively. The green and blue curves show the results of NA-QAS without ternary Gray-code implicit mapping and ZX topological reuse under noisy and noiseless conditions, respectively.

FIG. 4. Relation between ZX topological complexity and molecular ground-state energy error. Panels (a), (b), and (c) show the results for H2, LiH, and H4, respectively. The main plots show the distribution of candidate-ansatz errors as a function of the spider count after ZX simpliﬁcation. The insets show box plots of the error distributions for ZX-QAS and Original QAS. Orange points denote the proposed ZX-QAS, while blue points denote Original QAS without ternary Gray-code implicit mapping and ZX topological reuse.

FIG. 5. Generational evolution of the ZX topological reuse ratio. Panels (a), (b), and (c) show the results for H2, LiH, and H4, respectively. The population size is 20 in each generation. Green bars denote new circuit topologies that require evaluation, while blue bars denote redundant circuit topologies identiﬁed by the ZX topological reuse mechanism.
